fr:mainmatter.html:p: In type theory, a system has inductive type if it can create new types from constants and functions that create terms of that type. Inductive types usually come with a function to prove properties about them.
In previous post, we have seen the basic inference rules of type theory. Now we will see the definition of natural numbers as an inductive type. Refer to HoTT Book and Egbert Rijke's.
In classical mathematics, the Peano axioms are a set of axioms for the natural numbers, an important object in mathematics.
In type theory, the type \mathbb {N} of natural number is an inductive type. Just like in dependent function type, we need four inference rules to define the natural numbers.
Now let's use the type theoretical induction principle of \mathbb {N} to perform some basic construction over \mathbb {N}.

We define addition over \mathbb {N} using the type theoretical induction principle of \mathbb {N}.
\text {add}_\mathbb {N} : \mathbb {N} \to (\mathbb {N} \to \mathbb {N})
which satisfies the following specification:
\begin {align*} \text {add}_\mathbb {N}(n, 0)&:\equiv n \\ \text {add}_\mathbb {N}(m,\text {succ}(n))&:\equiv \text {succ}(\text {add}_\mathbb {N}(m,n)) \end {align*}
abbreviated as m + n for \text {add}_\mathbb {N}(m,n).

The Fibonacci function is a well-known function in mathematics. It is defined by pattern matching on the variable n as follows:
\begin {align*} \text {fib}(0) & :\equiv 0 \\ \text {fib}(1) & :\equiv 1 \\ \text {fib}(n+2) & :\equiv \text {fib}(n) + \text {fib}(n+1) \end {align*}
